author: reek
body: Algebraic simplification engine. Applies rewrite rules repeatedly until a fixed point (the expression stops changing). Rules include constant folding, identity elimination, commutativity normalization, power rules, log/exp cancellation, and trigonometric identities. Each rule is a pattern match on the expression tree.

author: reek
body: Every identity rule tests an operand against a literal integer, so these read as an ordered if-chain over one predicate. The chain is in the same order the arms were, which matters: ExMul of -1 and 0 must give 0, because the zero rule was written above the negation rule.

author: reek
body: sqrt of a perfect square folds to the root. The quadratic solver builds ExSqrt directly rather than through the ex-sqrt smart constructor, so without this rule `solve-quadratic 1 (-5) 6` prints `x = (5 + sqrt(1)) / 2 or x = (5 - sqrt(1)) / 2` instead of `x = 3 or x = 2`.

author: reek
body: One behaviour change, deliberate and called out. The quotient power rule x^n / x^m = x^(n-m) was written as its own arm BELOW the general `ExDiv (a) (b)` equality arm, and that arm matches every ExDiv and answers `e` when the sides differ -- so the power rule could never fire. It is now reached from that arm's else branch, which is plainly what it was written to do. The product rule above it was always reachable and is unchanged.

author: reek
body: The rewrite loop is fuel-capped. It used to recurse until a step compared equal to its input, with nothing bounding it, so a rule that failed to converge -- or an ex-equal that could not recognise its own output, which is exactly what happened with ExFn -- ran forever on a machine with no GC and no scheduler to interrupt it. The cap is far above what any convergent expression needs, so it changes no answer that was previously returned; it only bounds one that was not.
